desc: The only thorough congressional investigation ever made of the United States intelligence system, and the benchmark this board's oversight view has lacked. Eleven senators, a hundred staff, more than eight hundred interviews and over a hundred and ten thousand pages of documents. It is carried here for what its own final report concedes rather than for what it achieved: that it never once examined an agency's files on its own, that the CIA and other executive agencies limited its access to the record, and that three chapters of its published findings, including the chapter on budgetary oversight, were deleted at the request of the agencies it was investigating. Two Michels-corpus speakers who agree on almost nothing else, Michael Shellenberger and Mick West, each name the committee as the template for a successful congressional penetration of a compartmented programme. The committee's own report says the penetration was mediated throughout, and that is the finding.

dossier.denialPosture: The board carries one denial link on this node and does not assert its direction, because the record does not establish one. What the record does establish is a self-report: the committee's own final report names the Central Intelligence Agency and other executive-branch agencies as having limited its access to the full record, in some instances by asserting executive privilege, and records that three chapters were deleted at the agencies' request. That is a committee describing what was done to it, published in the document the agencies reviewed before it went out. The board treats it as a documented behaviour with the direction left open, rather than converting a self-report into a directed act.
dossier.narrative:
The committee is carried here for what it concedes rather than for what it achieved, and the concession is in its own words: 'Despite its legal Senate mandate, and the issuance of subpoenas, in no instance has the Committee been able to examine the agencies' files on its own. In all the agencies, whether CIA, FBI, NSA, INR, DIA, or the NSC, documents and evidence have been presented through the filter of the agency itself.' That sentence is the sharpest statement on this board of the structural problem every subsequent oversight claim inherits. Subpoena power did not produce unmediated access. What reached the Senate was what the holder of the file elected to hand over.

The money follows the same pattern twice. Among the committee's findings: 'Congress' failure as a whole to monitor the intelligence agencies' expenditures has been a major element in the ineffective legislative oversight of the intelligence community,' and more broadly that 'Mechanisms for, and the practice of, congressional oversight have not been adequate.' The committee recommended annual publication of the aggregate national intelligence figure. Then the published report's own note records that 'At the request of the agencies, the Committee deleted three chapters from this report: "Cover," "Espionage," and "Budgetary Oversight."' The chapter on budgetary oversight was removed at the request of the agencies whose budgets it examined. Two sections of the covert-action chapter and one section of the State Department chapter went the same way.

The board uses this node as a calibration point. When a witness says a compartmented programme can be reached by a determined congressional committee, this is the strongest instance available, and it is documented failing on exactly the two axes that matter to this board: file access and money. What it did produce was permanent. It recommended the standing oversight committee that followed it, and the record of its own obstruction survives in the published volumes because the committee chose to print the obstruction alongside the findings.
openQuestions: The three deleted chapters, 'Cover', 'Espionage' and 'Budgetary Oversight', have not been located in any later release. The board knows they existed and knows who asked for their removal, and holds none of their text.
The board reads Book I directly and Book III through the Angleton citations. Books II, IV, V and VI have not been opened for this node.

The succession to the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence is graded Tier 2 because the establishing resolution was not opened. The committee's own report refers throughout to 'any successor oversight committee', which is intent, not enactment.
dossier.whatItIs: The Senate Select Committee to Study Governmental Operations with Respect to Intelligence Activities, established by Senate Resolution 21 on 27 January 1975 'to conduct an investigation and study of governmental operations with respect to intelligence activities and of the extent, if any, to which illegal, improper, or unethical activities were engaged in by any agency of the Federal Government.' Eleven senators, six from the majority and five from the minority, chaired by Frank Church of Idaho with John G. Tower of Texas as Vice Chairman. A staff of 100, including 60 professionals, conducted more than 800 interviews and over 250 executive hearings across documentation in excess of 110,000 pages. Book I of the final report, Senate Report 94-755, was filed on 26 April 1976.
dossier.whyImplicated: It is the benchmark, and it is the benchmark's own limit case. Two speakers in the Michels corpus who agree on almost nothing else, Michael Shellenberger and Mick West, each name this committee as the model for what congressional penetration of a compartmented programme should look like. The committee's report describes a penetration that was mediated at every step. It never once examined an agency's files on its own. The CIA and other executive agencies limited its access to the full record, in some instances by asserting executive privilege. And three chapters of its findings, one of them the chapter on budgetary oversight, were deleted from the published report at the request of the agencies it was investigating. The most thorough inquiry ever made into the American intelligence system reported that it could not see the files and could not publish what it found about the money.
